Unit Testing the Service Layer

Testing ticket.service.js in isolation — no HTTP, no server, just a function call and a value back.

ticket.service.js (Figure 1.9, services-as-a-layer topic) is exactly the kind of code a unit test suits best: plain functions, no database, no network — call one, get a value back. A test file can import those functions directly, the same way ticket.controller.js does, and call them exactly as they are:

// Figure 1.14: unit-testing the service layer (tests/unit/ticket.service.test.js, excerpt)
import { getTicketById, createTicket } from '../../src/services/ticket.service.js';

describe('ticket.service', () => {
  it('getTicketById returns undefined for an unknown id', async () => {
    const ticket = await getTicketById(999);

    expect(ticket).toBeUndefined();
  });

  it('createTicket adds a new ticket with status "open"', async () => {
    const ticket = await createTicket({
      subject: 'New issue',
      description: 'Details',
    });

    expect(ticket).toMatchObject({
      subject: 'New issue',
      description: 'Details',
      status: 'open',
    });
  });
});

Nothing here is new syntax — await getTicketById(999) is the same async/await from earlier in this lesson, just called from a test instead of a controller. What's new is the pair of matchers: .toBeUndefined() checks for exactly that value (the documented behaviour when no ticket matches), and .toMatchObject({...}) checks that the result contains the given fields, without demanding an exact match on every property (handy here since createTicket also assigns an id this test doesn't want to hardcode).

This is what makes it a unit test rather than an integration test: no app, no route, no HTTP verb anywhere — just the one function, in isolation. That's also why it's possible to write today, a full week before Prisma and a real database exist. When ticket.service.js does become real MySQL queries from Week 2 onward, this test's shape barely changes — it still just calls getTicketById and checks what comes back.
